strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: steering methods are evaluated inconsistently, and cross-behavior entanglement is largely unmeasured. The distinction between primary (steered) and secondary (side-effect) behaviors is a useful framing, and the finding that prior work's reliance on TruthfulQA-style evaluation masks larger entanglement effects on social behaviors (sycophancy, anthropomorphism) is a genuinely valuable empirical insight.

The collection of 17 datasets spanning harmful generation, bias, and hallucination, plus 10 secondary behaviors across four categories, provides broad and reusable evaluation infrastructure, with sensible stratified 40/10/50 splits and negative-example construction for contrastive direction generation.

The modular taxonomy of steering components (direction generation, selection, application) is well-conceived and cleanly implemented across five representative methods (DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, LAT), enabling standardized comparison and easy extension to other combinations.

The three evaluation variants (Standard, No KL, Conditional/CAST) form a meaningful ablation of the entanglement-performance tradeoff, and the Pareto analysis in Figure 2 plus per-behavior heatmaps (Figures 3-8) give a fairly complete picture of the results.

The limitations section is honest and thorough (English-only, static vectors, uniform grid search, 64-token generation, no thinking mode, last-token-only directions), and code is released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scale of evaluation is narrow: only two ~7-8B instruction-tuned models, both English. The central claims ('strong steering performance is dependent on the specific combination of method, model, and behavior') are drawn from just two models, and no statistical significance, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported for any result.

The 'dynamic testing strategy' of evaluating on a 20% subset of each dataset is under-motivated and underspecified: how the subset is sampled, whether it is fixed across methods, and whether it is representative is unclear. It also sits awkwardly with the stated concern about overfitting and weakens statistical power.

Metric design has issues that merit more justification. ENTANGLEMENT (Eq. 2) uses an RMSE of performance changes, which counts beneficial out-of-distribution improvements as entanglement; this design choice is not defended. EFFECTIVENESS normalizes by (1-y), which makes target-behavior gains on near-floor baselines (e.g., SALAD ASR at 1.3%) appear very large. The treatment of directionality (higher-is-better vs. lower-is-better datasets like ASR and Political Views) inside these aggregate formulas is not spelled out.

Grid search selects directions using the benchmark's own validation sets with a KL check on Alpaca only; there is a risk of benchmark-specific tuning, and the Alpaca-based KL filter may be a poor proxy for preserving general behavior across the diverse secondary tasks. The sensitivity of results to the KL threshold (10%) is not analyzed.

Several judging pipelines rely on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o for DarkBench behaviors and Sneaking, LLaMA-3.3-70B for hallucination rate, LlamaGuard-4 for refusal, GPT-4o for filtering SALADBench) without any reported human validation or judge-reliability analysis, which is a notable gap for a paper whose contribution is measurement.

Relative to existing infrastructure (AxBench, EasyEdit2, Im & Li 2025), the novelty is incremental: the main differentiators are the entanglement focus and broader secondary behaviors. The empirical findings are largely qualitative ('methods differ by model and behavior'; 'CAST reduces entanglement') without deeper analysis of why entanglement arises, e.g., the proposed 'shared mechanisms in prompt interpretation' hypothesis is stated but not tested.

Presentation issues: the aggregate Pareto figure (Figure 2) is small and hard to read, key quantitative aggregate results are not tabulated, the GitHub link is incomplete in the manuscript, and choices such as the coefficient range (-3 to 3), the 25th-80th percentile layer search, and applying directions at last-token position only are arbitrary and acknowledged as such but not ablated.

strengths: The core idea is valuable and well-motivated: systematically measuring behavioral entanglement (unintended side effects) of activation steering on a broad suite of primary and secondary alignment behaviors, beyond the TruthfulQA-style checks used in prior work (e.g., Arditi et al., 2024).

The modular decomposition of training-free steering into direction generation, selection, and application components is a useful conceptual contribution, and re-expressing five popular methods (DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, LAT) within a common framework enables more controlled comparison.

The dataset collection is substantial (17 datasets spanning refusal, bias, hallucination, plus secondary behaviors), with reasonable documentation of splits, negative-example construction, and scoring procedures.

CAST-style conditional steering is integrated as an entanglement-mitigation variant, and the paper reports useful findings, e.g., that entanglement shows up more in social behaviors (sycophancy, anthropomorphism) than in reasoning benchmarks.
The limitations section is honest and specific (English-only, static vectors, 64-token generations, uniform grid search), which is appropriate treatment of scope.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is too small to support the central claims: only two models (Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), yet the paper concludes that steering performance is 'dependent on the specific combination of steering method, model, and targeted behavior.' Two models cannot establish model-dependence; no larger models, no variance over seeds.

No statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed variance anywhere, despite many reported deltas of 1-3% on secondary datasets with only 110 prompts (DarkBench-based tasks). Many of the entanglement findings could be noise.

The 'dynamic testing strategy' (Section 2.1) is poorly justified: evaluating steering only on a 20% subset of each dataset does not 'reduce the likelihood of overfitting to static evaluation sets' — it simply reduces sample size and statistical power. The reasoning conflating subsampling with robustness is unsound.

The ENTANGLEMENT metric (Eq. 2) aggregates absolute performance shifts via RMS, penalizing beneficial shifts on secondary behaviors equally with harmful ones. This conflates 'entanglement' with any OOD sensitivity, and the EFFECTIVENESS normalization by (1 - y_b) is not motivated or analyzed. The metrics' properties are never examined.

Heavy reliance on LLM judges (GPT-4o for social behaviors and sneaking, LlamaGuard-4 for refusal, LLaMA-3.3-70B for factuality) with no validation of judge agreement, calibration, or susceptibility to steering-induced format changes — a serious concern since steering vectors are known to alter response style, which could masquerade as behavior change.

The reimplementations deviate from original methods (standardized grid search, forced component choices 'where it isn't clear'), so reported method rankings may reflect the authors' standardized pipeline rather than the methods as published; there is no sanity-check against original results or AxBench numbers.

The headline Pareto analysis (Figure 2) presents scattered points rather than identifiable Pareto curves, and the aggregate metrics obscure exactly the per-behavior nuances the paper argues are important; the appendix heatmaps do most of the real evidential work.

Reproducibility is undermined in the manuscript itself: the released code URL in the abstract is an incomplete 'https://github.com/' link. Details needed for reproduction (judge prompts, KL check threshold calibration, direction-selection objective details) are thin or deferred.

Dual-use concerns (the benchmark explicitly steers models toward harmful generation / jailbreaking) are not addressed in an ethics discussion; the limitations section does not cover potential misuse of released steering directions.

Some evaluation choices are questionable: Political Views is scored as 'percentage choosing left-leaning option' with an acknowledged arbitrary direction, yet it is folded into aggregate entanglement; TwinViews results are silently dropped for Llama, breaking comparability of entanglement across models.

strengths: Addresses a real and timely gap: representation steering methods are evaluated with incompatible datasets, directions, and metrics, and this paper provides a standardized benchmark (17 datasets spanning 3 primary safety behaviors and 10 secondary behaviors) plus a modular framework decomposing steering methods into direction generation, selection, and application components. This taxonomy-driven design makes the comparison of DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT on equal footing genuinely useful.

The effectiveness-vs-entanglement framing is a valuable conceptual contribution. Prior work (e.g., Arditi et al.) examined side effects mainly on TruthfulQA/reasoning, whereas this paper shows larger entanglement on social behaviors (sycophancy, anthropomorphism) and between primary targets, and demonstrates that conditional steering (CAST) often dominates the Pareto frontier. These are actionable findings for the field.

The modular code framework and public release of datasets (with fixed train/val/test splits and negative examples for contrastive direction generation) substantially improve reproducibility and lower the barrier for future steering-method evaluation.

The limitations section (Section 7) is unusually thorough and honest: English-only data, static vectors, uniform grid search, 64-token generation limits, aggregate reporting, and non-final-token directions are all acknowledged candidly and with relevant citations.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is insufficient for the central claims. No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere, despite evaluation sets being small in places (e.g., 110 DarkBench prompts per secondary behavior) and primary evaluations being run on only a 20% subset 'for computational cost'. Several headline claims (e.g., PCA vs. LAT ordering in Figure 2, model-specific failures) rest on differences of a few percentage points that could plausibly be noise. The 'dynamic testing' justification for subsetting is asserted but not empirically supported (e.g., no comparison of subset vs. full-set stability).

Generalization claims outrun the evidence: with only two models (Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), the conclusion that 'steering performance is dependent on the specific combination of steering method, model, and targeted behavior' is plausible but weakly supported, and the claim that 'models are a key determinant' cannot be separated from scale/family confounds. A third model, ideally a different scale or family, would materially strengthen the paper.

The aggregate metrics are under-justified. Effectiveness (Eq. 1) normalizes by y(1−y), which amplifies changes near extremes, but no analysis of how this affects cross-dataset aggregation is given. Entanglement (Eq. 2) is the RMS of absolute changes, so it penalizes beneficial side effects equally with harmful ones and cannot distinguish benign performance shifts from damage; a signed or directional treatment (or at least a discussion) is needed since the paper's central theme is entanglement.

Heavy reliance on LLM judges (GPT-4o for social behaviors and sneaking, LlamaGuard-4 for refusal, LLaMA-3.3-70B for factuality) with no validation of judge agreement, position bias, or consistency under the steered models' potentially degraded outputs. Since steering can distort generation style, judge reliability under intervention is exactly where validation matters most.

Some methodological choices are hard to assess and possibly confound comparisons: a uniform grid search (layers at 25th–80th quantile, coefficients −3 to 3) is applied to all methods although some methods may need different tuning; the KL-divergence-on-Alpaca check (10% threshold) differs across variants in ways that entangle method and selection-procedure effects; the decision to exclude TwinViews only for Llama is a post-hoc fix that hints at fragile evaluation infrastructure.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: the main quantitative results live in dense small-font appendix heatmaps (Figures 3–8) that are hard to read; Figure 3/4 captions mention 'five objectives' while Section 4 describes three primary steering interventions; there is no calibration against prior benchmark results (e.g., AxBench), which would help readers judge whether the standardized implementations are faithful to the original methods.

Coverage gaps relative to the paper's framing: despite discussing AxBench's finding that simple baselines outperform SAE-based steering, no SAE-based or training-based steering (ReFT) baseline is included, so the benchmark's claim of 'holistic' coverage of the steering paradigm is only partially realized (acknowledged in limitations, but it narrows the contribution).

strengths: Comprehensive and well-scoped benchmark: 9 safety perspectives, 18 datasets, 5 steering methods, 5 models, and 3 steering settings (280+ experiments), with full pipeline details (hyperparameters in Tables 5-15, dataset splits in Table 3, judge prompts in Appendix E) supporting reproducibility.

Careful metric design with explicit justification: headroom-normalized Effectiveness (Eq. 1) prevents gains on low-baseline perspectives from being conflated with gains on high-baseline ones, and the choice to report unnormalized Entanglement drift is transparently argued and contextualized.

Rigorous treatment of empirical uncertainty: FDR-corrected paired t-tests on all per-dataset results, human-LLM judge agreement analysis (Cohen's κ of 0.86-0.92 for PreciseWikiQA and SALAD-Bench), and a signed entanglement decomposition (Appendix G.1) that separates harmful from beneficial drift, adding analytical depth beyond raw benchmark numbers.

Honest and careful claims: the mechanistic account in Section 5 is explicitly framed as a candidate hypothesis rather than a finding; the refusal-induction direction is omitted with clear justification; multiple causal accounts for method differences are presented as non-identifiable rather than asserted.

Actionable empirical findings: conditional (CAST) steering yields Pareto improvements on refusal and hallucination but fails on bias; social behaviors are consistently most entangled while reasoning is robust; jailbreaking does not uniformly increase toxicity. These are useful, evidence-supported observations for practitioners.
Thorough limitations section (Appendix A) covering English-only data, static vectors, method reproduction ambiguity, aggregation effects, LLM judges, and token-position choices.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely descriptive. The paper deliberately avoids mechanistic attribution (Section 5) and offers no new steering method; novelty relative to existing frameworks (AxBench, EasyEdit2) is mainly the systematic cross-perspective entanglement measurement, which is incremental in methodological terms even if valuable.

Method comparisons are confounded by design choices. The five methods differ not only in direction generation but also in application mechanism, position, and location (Table 1), and prompt formatting varies per method (default/RepE/CAA); the paper acknowledges but does not disentangle whether observed method differences reflect direction-generation differences or application differences.

Several key headline claims rest on small or noisy measurements: DarkBench subsets have only ~110 test examples each, yet 'up to 76% degradation' in social behaviors (from NoKL settings) is a headline result; judge-based metrics on such small sets make the social-behavior conclusions indicative at best, as the authors themselves concede.

Scale is limited to 2B-8B instruction-tuned models, and generalization is only checked within the Qwen family; the paper's central finding that entanglement is determined by the (method, model, perspective) triple may not transfer to larger or frontier models, limiting significance.

Steering effectiveness on hallucination and bias is modest and inconsistent across methods and models, so a substantial portion of the benchmark grid consists of near-null results; the practical guidance for these perspectives is correspondingly weak.

Dependence on LLM-as-a-judge for several perspectives (SALAD-Bench, PreciseWikiQA, all DarkBench datasets) introduces potential judge-side bias; DarkBench agreement (κ ≈ 0.71) is only cited from prior work rather than independently verified on the steered outputs, where distribution shift may degrade judge reliability.

Some results are hard to interpret due to dataset-specific idiosyncrasies, e.g., TwinViews has very high invalid-answer rates (35-75%) for Gemma and Llama, requiring a likelihood-based scoring switch mid-analysis; similar switches weaken comparability across perspectives.

strengths: Comprehensive scope and real gap filled: the benchmark systematically measures cross-perspective entanglement of representation steering across 9 safety perspectives, 18 datasets, 5 methods, and 5 models (including two additional Qwen sizes for scale-consistency checks), which prior frameworks (AxBench, EasyEdit2) do not evaluate at this breadth.

Empirically rigorous: FDR-corrected paired t-tests with significance markers, human-LLM judge agreement validation (Cohen's kappa 0.86-0.92 on SALAD-Bench and PreciseWiki), and a signed harm/benefit decomposition of entanglement (Appendix G.1) that adds real analytical value beyond aggregate drift.

Careful methodological hygiene: the effectiveness metric normalization by remaining headroom is justified, the decision not to normalize entanglement is explicitly argued rather than hidden, baseline drifts are always shown, invalid-answer rates are transparently reported (Table 18), and the TwinViews substring-matching failure is handled by likelihood scoring with justification.

Useful actionable findings: conditional steering (CAST) achieves Pareto improvements in most but not all settings (with an honest analysis of why it fails on bias), the effectiveness/entanglement ratio table gives practitioners concrete method-model pairings, and counterintuitive results (jailbreaking not uniformly increasing toxicity, opposing political shifts across models) are well-supported by the heatmap data.

Thorough reproducibility documentation: full hyperparameter grids, per-experiment selected layers/coefficients/thresholds (Tables 5-15), judge prompts, dataset splits and sizes, and compute estimates are all provided.

Honest limitations section covering English-only data, static vectors, LLM-judge bias (with DarkBench agreement explicitly flagged as weaker), and method reproduction choices; the mechanistic 'superposition' explanation is appropriately framed as a candidate hypothesis rather than a claim.
weaknesses: Purely descriptive contribution: the paper introduces no new steering method or algorithmic insight, and its headline findings (entanglement is model/perspective-dependent, social behaviors are fragile) largely formalize phenomena already reported anecdotally in prior work; the value rests almost entirely on scale and systematization.

The mechanistic interpretation section (Section 5) is essentially unrewarding: the superposition hypothesis is acknowledged as untestable with the presented evidence, so the paper offers hypotheses that are explicitly 'not separately identifiable from our data,' leaving the central 'why' question open.

Dependence on LLM judges for several headline findings: sycophancy/retention/anthropomorphism (GPT-4o) and political views shifts are central to the claims, yet DarkBench judge agreement (~0.71 kappa) is comparatively weak, and the authors themselves instruct readers to treat these conclusions as 'indicative trends' — which weakens some of the strongest-sounding claims in the abstract.

Some perspective definitions are heterogeneous and loosely coupled to the construct (e.g., 'refusal' measured solely as attack success rate under suppression; 'normative judgment' mixing commonsense morality with political leaning), and small test sets for DarkBench subsets (109-110 prompts) limit sensitivity for several reported entanglement cells.
Citation hygiene issues: several references are dated 2026 with impossible arXiv identifiers (e.g., arXiv:2604.19784), which undermines confidence in reference diligence.

The code footnote on page 1 is empty in the provided manuscript, so reproducibility of the modular framework could not be verified from the submission itself; dataset curation steps (GPT-4o filtering of SALAD-Bench, GPT-4.1-mini negative generation) also introduce pipeline steps whose quality is asserted rather than independently validated.

strengths: Comprehensive scope: the benchmark covers nine safety perspectives across 18 datasets, five steering methods, and five models (including two additional Qwen scales), which is substantially broader than prior steering evaluation efforts (AxBench, EasyEdit2) and directly targets the under-measured problem of cross-perspective entanglement.

Careful metric design and honest discussion of its limitations: Effectiveness is normalized by remaining headroom to make gains comparable across baselines, while the authors deliberately avoid normalizing Entanglement and clearly explain why (Section 3.2), and they add a signed decomposition showing 84.3% of entanglement is harmful (Appendix G.1), which strengthens interpretability.

Empirical rigor: FDR-corrected paired t-tests with significance markers, baseline-relative deltas on every per-dataset figure, hyperparameter tables for all ~274 experiments, and a human–LLM judge agreement study (Cohen's κ of 0.86–0.92 for PreciseWiki and SALAD-Bench) that anticipates and addresses judge-bias concerns.

Practically useful analysis beyond raw numbers: the effectiveness–entanglement tradeoff ratios (Table 2), comparison of Standard/NoKL/Conditional settings showing CAST-style gating reduces entanglement (Finding 4), and scale-consistency checks in the Qwen family give actionable guidance to practitioners.

Intellectual honesty: Section 5 explicitly frames the superposition account as a non-established candidate hypothesis, mechanistic causal claims are disclaimed, and the limitations appendix (Appendix A) candidly covers English-only data, judge bias, 64-token generation limits, and reproduction ambiguity of original methods.

Good treatment of the refusal asymmetry: the paper explains and justifies benchmarking only refusal suppression (adversarial robustness) rather than refusal induction, citing known saturation effects and near-floor baselines.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily descriptive; the central findings (entanglement is method–model–perspective dependent, social behaviors are most vulnerable, reasoning is robust) are plausible and partially anticipated by prior SFT/RLHF interference results, so the analytical novelty beyond systematizing measurement is moderate.

Findings rest on relatively small models (2B–8B) from three families; it is unclear whether the entanglement patterns and method rankings transfer to larger frontier-scale models, which limits the practical reach of the conclusions (acknowledged only indirectly via the Qwen-scale check within one family).

A meaningful share of results depend on LLM-as-judge evaluation (DarkBench behaviors use GPT-4o with only ~0.71 κ borrowed from prior work), and the paper itself notes DarkBench conclusions should be read as indicative trends; key findings about the most entangled perspectives (social behaviors, normative judgment) are precisely in this lower-reliability regime.

Some headline numbers feel fragile to setup choices: steering coefficients are restricted to integers [-3,3], layers to the 25th–80th percentile with step 2, and 64-token generations; the paper concedes that alternative reproduction choices (e.g., for LAT) were possible, so specific per-cell conclusions may not be robust.

Hallucination and bias steering show low or near-zero effectiveness in many cells (e.g., extrinsic hallucination essentially unsteerable in two of three main models), which weakens the evidential basis for entanglement claims in those regimes; near-zero effectiveness paired with nonzero entanglement ratios (e.g., LAT bias 7.05 'despite low absolute effectiveness') is difficult to interpret practically.

The aggregated Effectiveness/Entanglement ratio conflates sign and mixes perspectives with very different scales; per-perspective signed breakdowns help (Table 16), but the main tradeoff tables can obscure whether a high ratio reflects genuinely safe steering or a small numerator/denominator artifact.

The code footnote on page 1 appears incomplete in the manuscript, and although the modular framework is a claimed contribution, reproducibility of the full pipeline (dataset curation with GPT-4o filtering of SALAD-Bench, negative example generation) depends on artifacts not fully verifiable from the text.
